result.rationale: In parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts the diff defines minimumTokenResponseSchema with computed keys `[z.string().toString()]: z.number()` and `[z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional()`. Zod schema objects do not override toString, so both computed keys evaluate to the literal string "[object Object]", not a dynamic key. The resulting schema only recognizes `access_token` (plus a junk "[object Object]" key), and since Zod strips unknown keys by default, safeParse's output drops fields like expiry_date, refresh_token, and token_type when credential-sync mode is on. This schema is us

adjudication.rationale: In `packages/app-store/_utils/oauth/parseRefreshTokenResponse.ts`, `minimumTokenResponseSchema` is defined as `z.object({ access_token: ..., [z.string().toString()]: z.number(), [z.string().optional().toString()]: z.unknown().optional() })`. Those computed property names are evaluated immediately and become a single literal key string (e.g. "[object Object]" / "ZodString"), not a wildcard/dynamic key matcher. As a result, when credential-sync mode is enabled, `minimumTokenResponseSchema.safeParse(response)` will not validate typical OAuth token responses (which have keys like `expiry_date`, `expires_in`, etc.), because it will require that one literal computed key to be present with a number. This can cause refresh flows that call `parseRefreshTokenResponse` (e.g. Google Calendar and Office365 in the diff) to throw `Invalid refreshed tokens were returned` at runtime. The finding’s core claim (schema is broken due to `.toString()` computed keys) is verifiable from the diff, though the exact failure mode is more likely a parse failure than “silently strips all other fields.”
